name: medintel-starter-kb
description: Starter knowledge base for the MedIntel prototype: short summaries of public CDC, NIH and MedlinePlus pages, each with its source.

review.note: Medical content must be checked by the team and Prof. G. P Mohole before use. Not clinical guidance.

passages.title: Severely high blood pressure (above 180/120 mm Hg)
passages.passage: NHLBI treats a reading above 180/120 mm Hg as too high and in need of medical attention, especially with symptoms, because pressure at this level can damage organs. Without symptoms, it advises rechecking after 5 minutes and calling a provider if the value stays high. If the repeat is still high with a sudden severe headache, sudden severe chest, back or abdominal pain, trouble breathing, numbness or weakness, a sudden vision change or trouble speaking, call 9-1-1 without waiting.

passages.title: Adult blood pressure categories
passages.passage: Following ACC and AHA guidelines, CDC describes adult blood pressure as normal when below 120/80 mm Hg and elevated when systolic is 120-129 mm Hg with diastolic under 80 mm Hg. Hypertension means readings that stay at or above 130/80 mm Hg: a systolic of 130 mm Hg or more, or a diastolic of 80 mm Hg or more. The higher the pressure, the greater the risk of heart disease, heart attack and stroke.

passages.title: Confirming a high blood pressure reading
passages.passage: Blood pressure rises and falls with activity, caffeine, alcohol, tobacco, posture and some medicines, so MedlinePlus notes that high blood pressure is usually diagnosed only after two or more high readings on different days. Readings are more accurate after at least 30 minutes without exercise, alcohol, tobacco or caffeine, with the person seated, feet flat, arm at heart level and a well-fitting cuff. Nervousness at a clinic visit (white coat syndrome) can raise readings temporarily.

passages.title: Healthy cholesterol levels and heart risk
passages.passage: For adults age 20 or older, MedlinePlus gives general healthy levels of total cholesterol less than 200 mg/dL and LDL less than 100 mg/dL; HDL is best at 60 mg/dL or more and low below 40 mg/dL in men or 50 mg/dL in women. For ages 19 or younger, healthy total cholesterol is less than 170 mg/dL. Too much blood cholesterol can narrow or block arteries, raising the risk of coronary artery disease.
passages.source_title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know

passages.title: Fasting blood sugar categories
passages.passage: The fasting plasma glucose test measures blood sugar after at least 8 hours without food or drink, with results in mg/dL. MedlinePlus lists 99 mg/dL or below as normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL as prediabetes and 126 mg/dL and above as type 2 diabetes. Even prediabetes brings a higher chance of developing heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes.

passages.title: Smoking, heart disease and the benefit of quitting
passages.passage: CDC reports that smoking causes one in every four deaths from cardiovascular disease and raises the risk of coronary heart disease and of stroke by 2 to 4 times each compared with not smoking. Risk falls quickly after quitting: heart attack risk drops sharply 1 to 2 years after quitting, the added coronary risk is halved after 3 to 6 years, and after 15 years coronary risk nears that of a nonsmoker.
passages.source_title: Health Effects of Cigarettes: Cardiovascular Disease

passages.title: Coronary heart disease risk factors
passages.passage: NHLBI notes that coronary heart disease risk grows with the number and severity of risk factors; high blood pressure, high cholesterol and smoking are the three key ones. Diabetes, overweight and obesity, and chronic kidney disease can also raise risk. Men's risk rises notably around age 45 and women's climbs faster around age 55; early heart disease in a father or brother before age 55, or a mother or sister before age 65, adds risk.

passages.title: Stable and unstable angina
passages.passage: Stable angina is chest pain or pressure that comes with physical activity or mental stress, keeps a pattern unchanged for 2 months, eases with rest and fades within 5 minutes. Unstable angina changes that pattern and can last longer than 20 minutes, come back, worsen or occur at rest; NHLBI advises calling 9-1-1 for chest discomfort that rest does not relieve. Women more often feel pain in the arms, neck, back or jaw, or have breathlessness, nausea or light-headedness.

passages.title: Heart attack warning signs
passages.passage: CDC lists the major heart attack symptoms as chest pain or discomfort that lasts more than a few minutes or returns; feeling weak, light-headed or faint; pain or discomfort in the jaw, neck, back, arms or shoulders; and shortness of breath. Unusual tiredness and nausea or vomiting can also occur and are more common in women. Anyone with these symptoms should call 9-1-1 right away, since faster treatment limits heart muscle damage.
passages.source_title: About Heart Attack Symptoms, Risk, and Recovery

passages.title: Exercise stress testing
passages.passage: Among the tests NHLBI lists for diagnosing coronary heart disease, a stress test examines the heart under exertion, usually while the person walks or runs on a treadmill or pedals a stationary bike. An ECG tracks the heart's electrical activity during exercise, and the ECG or an imaging test is used to look for reduced blood flow to the heart muscle.

passages.title: Nuclear heart scan with stress imaging
passages.passage: A nuclear heart scan uses a radioactive tracer and special cameras to show whether parts of the heart are not getting blood flow, which helps diagnose coronary heart disease. Images are taken right after a stress test, because some problems appear only when the heart works hard, and again once the heartbeat is back to normal. The scan can also reveal damaged or dead heart muscle, possibly from an earlier heart attack.

passages.title: Coronary angiography by cardiac catheterization
passages.passage: Coronary angiography is performed through cardiac catheterization: a catheter is guided into the coronary arteries, contrast dye usually containing iodine is injected through it, and X-ray pictures reveal blockages caused by plaque buildup. NHLBI says it helps diagnose heart disease and may follow abnormal results from an EKG or exercise stress test.

passages.title: Thickened heart muscle from high blood pressure
passages.passage: NHLBI names high blood pressure, along with other conditions that force the heart to work harder, as a main cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The heart muscle gradually thickens in response and becomes stiffer, so the left side of the heart cannot relax fully between beats or fill with enough blood. Obesity and diabetes can also stiffen the heart's chambers.
passages.source_title: Heart Failure Causes and Risk Factors

passages.title: Fast resting heart rate (tachycardia)
passages.passage: NHLBI defines tachycardia as a resting heart rate faster than 100 beats per minute, above the usual adult resting range of 60 to 100 beats per minute, and it may come with an irregular heartbeat. Fast rhythms that begin in the ventricles can be very dangerous and usually need medical care right away; ventricular tachycardia lasting more than a few seconds can lead to ventricular fibrillation.

passages.title: Creatinine, GFR and kidney disease
passages.passage: Kidney function is checked with a blood test for glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which providers estimate from the level of creatinine, a muscle waste product that climbs as kidney disease worsens. GFR values of 60 or higher fall in the normal range, values below 60 may mean kidney disease, and 15 or less is classed as kidney failure. NIDDK advises kidney testing for people with diabetes, high blood pressure or heart disease, or with relatives who had kidney failure.

passages.title: Blood pressure in children under 13
passages.passage: NHLBI advises a blood pressure check by a healthcare provider at least yearly for everyone age 3 or older. Whereas most adults are judged against fixed numbers, such as a healthy level below 120/80 mm Hg, children younger than 13 are measured against what is typical for children of their own age, sex and height. A cuff suited to the child's sex and age is also needed for accurate readings.

passages.title: Adult BMI categories and waist size
passages.passage: For adults, NHLBI defines BMI categories as underweight below 18.5, healthy weight 18.5 to 24.9, overweight 25 to 29.9 and obesity 30 or above. BMI is a screening tool that does not by itself diagnose body fatness, so waist size also counts: over 40 inches in men or 35 inches in women is unhealthy. Fat inside the abdomen (visceral fat) drives inflammation and adds to obesity-related problems such as heart disease and diabetes.
passages.source_title: Overweight and Obesity Symptoms and Diagnosis

passages.title: Healthy habits that lower heart disease risk
passages.passage: CDC says a healthy lifestyle helps keep blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar at normal levels and lowers the risk of heart disease and heart attack. Helpful habits include eating plenty of fruits and vegetables with less salt, sugar and saturated fat, keeping a healthy weight, not smoking (quitting lowers heart disease risk) and, for adults, 2 hours and 30 minutes of moderate-intensity activity each week.
